questions.q: Your code looks for tasks.ada in the cache and it is not there, so it asks the database. What is this called?
questions.explain: A miss means the value was not in the cache, so you do the slow work. A hit means the copy was there and you skipped the work.

questions.q: What is the main price you pay for caching?
questions.explain: A cached copy does not update itself. Most of the work of caching is keeping copies correct: how long they live, and removing them when the data changes.
options: The cache makes every request slower
A copy can be stale: the database changed but the cache still holds the old answer
The database can no longer be written to
Cached values are always converted to strings

questions.q: Which of these should you not cache?
questions.explain: If data must always be exact, like a bank balance or a permission check, a stale copy is a real bug or a security hole. Cache results where a short delay is acceptable.
options: A list of countries that changes once a year
A task list that you clear on every change
A permission check that must always be exact
A report that takes 3 seconds to build and changes daily

questions.q: In @zudojs/cache, what is the difference between the CacheService and the adapter?
questions.explain: You always call the service (get, set, getOrSet...). The adapter decides where entries live: memory now, a shared store such as Redis later, without changing your code.
options: They are two names for the same object
The service is the object you call; the adapter is the actual storage behind it, like the in-memory Map
The adapter is for reads and the service is for writes
The service runs in the browser and the adapter runs in Node

questions.q: A memory cache was created with maxEntries: 1000 and it is full. What happens when you store one more entry?
questions.explain: A cache is allowed to forget. When it is full, the least recently used entry makes room for the new one, and the next read of it is simply a miss.
options: The entry that was used least recently is dropped

questions.q: Why should you check found.hit instead of found.value?
questions.explain: An empty task list is a perfectly good cached answer. If you tested the value, you would treat it as a miss and query the database every time.
options: Because a cached value can itself be null or an empty list, which still counts as a hit
Because reading value counts as a second read

questions.q: Why does the key builder reject a key part such as "ada:tasks.list"?
questions.explain: The full key is prefix:namespace:key. If a key part could contain :, someone who controls part of a key could read or overwrite another user's entry.
options: Because colons make keys too long
The colon separates prefix, namespace and key, so it would look like another user's namespace and key
Because keys may only contain lowercase letters

questions.q: You cache GET /tasks under the key tasks.list, with no namespace. Ada asks first, then Linus. What happens?
questions.explain: The cache only knows the key. The key or namespace must include everything the answer depends on, especially the user, taken from the verified login token.
options: Linus gets his own tasks, because the cache knows who is logged in
Linus receives Ada's tasks: a data leak
The second request throws an error
Nothing is cached, because the key has no user

questions.q: Where should the user id for a cache namespace come from?
questions.explain: Anything the client can change, it can set to another user's id and read their cached data. Only the verified token tells you who is really asking.
options: A header the client sends, like X-User
The verified login token, as in the authentication lesson
A random value created for each request

questions.q: Why is a TTL called a safety net?
questions.explain: When the time is up, the entry counts as missing and the next read gets fresh data. Invalidation is the main tool; the TTL limits the damage when invalidation is missed.
options: It stops the cache from using too much memory
Even if you forget to clear an entry, it cannot stay wrong for longer than its TTL
It makes the database answer faster
It encrypts entries after a while

questions.q: You want a settings entry that never expires. What do you write?
questions.explain: ttl: null means "never expires". ttl: 0 is a common mistake: it is rejected with CACHE_INVALID_TTL.

questions.q: What happens when you make a TTL much longer?
questions.explain: A TTL is a trade-off between speed and freshness. Data you cannot clear reliably, like another company's API answer, should live only as long as you can accept it being out of date.
options: More hits and less database work, but stale data stays around longer
Fewer hits and more database work
The data can never be stale
Nothing changes, the TTL only affects memory

questions.q: What is a cache stampede?
questions.explain: 50 requests in the same millisecond all miss and all hit the database. getOrSet prevents it: other callers for the same key wait for the one running computation.
options: Too many different keys in the cache at once
An entry expires and many requests miss at the same moment, so they all run the same slow query
Two users writing to the same key
A cache that is cleared every second

questions.q: You run three copies of the Task API. How far does the stampede protection of getOrSet reach?
questions.explain: Waiting callers are tracked in each process's memory. One query per copy is usually fine; for "exactly once across servers" you need a lock in a shared store.
options: Across all servers, because the key is the same
Inside one process only; each copy can still run one query
It does not work at all with more than one copy

questions.q: Which rule keeps cached task lists correct?
questions.explain: Create, update, delete and any background job that changes tasks must clear the entries they made stale. Invalidating before every read would make the cache useless.
options: Clear the whole cache once an hour
Only read from the cache, never write to it
Every code path that writes the data also invalidates its cache entries, right after the write succeeds
Invalidate the cache before every read

questions.q: Why are tags often more useful than delete(key) for invalidation?
questions.explain: A new task changes the full list, the open list and the count. Tag them all with tasks, and a new cached view with that tag is cleared by the same code.
options: One change often makes several entries stale, and one tag clears them all without listing the keys
Tags also clear other users' entries

questions.q: You tagged Ada's entries with tasks in the namespace ada, then call invalidateByTag(["tasks"]) with no namespace. What happens?
questions.explain: Tags live inside a namespace. Pass the same namespace on both sides, or the stale list stays in the cache silently.
options: All of Ada's tagged entries are cleared
It throws an error about the missing namespace
Nothing is cleared, and no error is thrown
Every entry in every namespace is cleared

questions.q: Why do you give withLock a ttl?
questions.explain: A lock held by a dead process would block forever. The lease expires; while your function runs, it is renewed for you.
options: So the work inside runs faster
It makes the lock a lease: if the process crashes while holding it, the lock frees itself instead of blocking everyone forever
So the result of the work is cached for that long
So other callers skip the lock after that time

questions.q: What does config.failSilently: true do when the Redis cache server is down?
questions.explain: An outage should only make you slower. A bad key or a lock that cannot be taken still throws, because those are bugs in your code, not an outage.
options: A broken cache behaves like a miss: the request goes to the database and still succeeds, only slower
It hides every error, including bad keys
It turns the cache off forever

questions.q: A teammate writes cache.getOrSet("report", () => buildReport(user.role)). An admin asks first, then a normal user. What is the best fix?
questions.explain: The answer depends on the role, but the key does not. The normal user would receive the admin report. Check permission first, so a normal user never reaches admin data, and include the role in the key.
options: Give the entry a shorter TTL
Clear the cache after every admin request
Check the permission before reading the cache, and put the role in the key

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: get always returns { hit, value }. For a missing key, hit is false and value is null.

questions.q: The common mistake. What does this print?
questions.explain: The result object is never falsy, so if (!found) never runs and the cache never fills. Write if (!found.hit).
options:
load from the database
hit: false

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: An empty list is a real cached answer, so it is a hit. That is why you check hit and not the value.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The full key is prefix:namespace:key. The prefix is zudojs unless you set another one, like taskapi here.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Without a namespace the key is prefix:key. A key part with a colon is refused with a 400 cache error, because the colon is the separator.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The same key in two namespaces is two different entries. Clearing Ada's namespace does not touch Linus's.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A namespace is checked like a key part. A wildcard throws instead of quietly reaching every user's entries.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: cache.ttl returns the milliseconds left, null for an entry that never expires, and undefined for a missing key.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: ttl: 0 does not mean "forever". It is rejected. Write ttl: null for an entry that never expires.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The first call misses, runs load and stores the result. The next two read the copy, so cached is true and the loader ran only once.

questions.q: Five requests arrive at the same moment. What does this print?
questions.explain: While one computation for a key runs, other callers for the same key wait for it. Five answers, one query: no stampede.

questions.q: Ada adds a task, but nobody invalidates the cache. What does this print?
questions.explain: The "database" has 3 tasks, but the cache still serves the old list of 2 until the TTL runs out. Every write path must invalidate the entries it made stale.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Tags live inside a namespace. Without the namespace nothing is cleared, silently. With namespace: "ada", both entries go.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: tasks.* matches every key that starts with tasks., so the list and the open list are removed. profile does not match and stays.

questions.q: No serializer is configured. What does this print?
questions.explain: The memory adapter stores the object you give it, not a copy. Any later change shows up for every reader. A serializer such as JsonCacheSerializer gives each reader its own copy.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: With room for 2 entries, storing c drops the least recently used entry. a was just read, so b is the one that goes.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: "*" listens to every event type. The delete happened after unsubscribe(), so it was not recorded.

questions.q: The database is down. What does this print?
questions.explain: The error from the loader reaches your code, and nothing is stored, so the next read is a miss and can try again. A failure is never cached as an answer.

questions.q: Finish cachedTasks(userId) without getOrSet. Use cache.get with the user as the namespace. On a hit, return the value. On a miss, call loadTasks(userId), store the result with cache.set in the same namespace, and return it.
questions.explain: Check found.hit, not the value: Linus's empty list is a real answer and must count as a hit. The namespace keeps Ada's and Linus's lists apart.

questions.q: Finish list(userId) with cache.getOrSet. Use the key tasks.list, the user as the namespace, and the tag tasks. Return only the value.
questions.explain: getOrSet looks, loads on a miss and stores in one call. It returns { value, cached }, so return result.value.

questions.q: The list is cached with the tag tasks in the user's namespace. Finish create(userId, title): add the title to rows first, then invalidate the user's tasks tag so the next list is fresh.
questions.explain: Write first, then invalidate, and pass the same namespace the entry was stored in. Without the namespace, invalidateByTag clears nothing and the list stays stale.

questions.q: Write buildKey(prefix, namespace, key) by hand. Every part must match /^[a-zA-Z0-9._-]+$/; if one does not, throw an Error with the message Invalid key part: followed by the part. Join the parts with ":".
questions.explain: Checking every part with an allow-list stops a colon from faking another namespace, and stops a wildcard from reaching every user's entries.
questions.expected:
taskapi:ada:tasks.list
Invalid key part: x:tasks.list
Invalid key part: *

questions.q: Store ["Buy milk"] for Ada and ["Fix bug"] for Linus under the key tasks.list, each in their own namespace. Then clear only Ada's namespace. The program prints whether each entry still exists.
questions.explain: clear({ namespace }) removes only the entries in that namespace. Linus's entry is untouched.

questions.q: Store { theme: "dark" } under settings so it never expires, and ["Buy milk"] under tasks.list with a TTL of 60 seconds. The program prints the TTL of settings and the type of the TTL of tasks.list.
questions.explain: TTLs are in milliseconds, so 60 seconds is 60_000. "Never expires" is ttl: null, not 0.

questions.q: Create the cache so that it stores copies: pass a JsonCacheSerializer as config.serializer. Then the change to task after set must not reach the cache.
questions.explain: With a serializer, the value is turned into text on the way in and rebuilt on the way out, so each reader gets its own copy. JsonCacheSerializer also keeps Date objects as dates.

questions.q: Finish rebuild(who) so the work runs inside cache.withLock with the lock name report.daily and { ttl: 10_000 }. Log "<who> starts", wait 10 ms, log "<who> ends", and return who. The two calls must never overlap.
questions.explain: withLock takes the lock, runs the function and releases it, even if the function throws. B waits and retries until A releases the lock. Lock names are keys too, so write report.daily, not report:daily.
questions.expected:
A starts
A ends
B starts
B ends
[ 'A', 'B' ]

questions.q: Subscribe to cache.miss events and count them in misses. Unsubscribe after the reads. The program prints the count and the hit rate from getStats().
questions.explain: Two reads missed (Ada's first read and Linus's read) and two hit. Hit rate is hits divided by all reads: 2 of 4 is 0.5.

questions.q: Build stampede protection by hand. once(key, load) keeps running promises in the inFlight map: if one is already running for the key, return it; otherwise start load(), store the promise, and delete it from the map when it settles.
questions.explain: All three callers share one promise, so the query runs once. finally removes it afterwards, so a later call starts fresh. getOrSet does this for you inside one process.

questions.q: Write hitRate(hits, misses): hits divided by all reads. When there were no reads at all, return 0 instead of NaN.
questions.explain: A hit rate of 0.9 means 9 of 10 reads were served from the cache. 0 / 0 is NaN, so handle "no reads" first. A low rate hints at a TTL that is too short or keys that never repeat.
